question: What does published evidence (2023–2026) show about AI coding assistants' effect on developer productivity, and why do the findings disagree?

requirements.text: Reports controlled-experiment (RCT) evidence on task speed or output with AI coding assistants, with direction and size of effect.
Includes evidence that experienced developers working on familiar, mature codebases were NOT sped up or were slowed down.
Reports field, telemetry, or organisation-level observational evidence from real development settings.
Addresses effects on code quality, defects, security, or maintainability, not only speed.
Distinguishes perceived/self-reported productivity from measured productivity.
Identifies moderators of the effect (developer experience, task type, codebase familiarity/size).
Explains how differences in outcome measures and study design (task completion time, PR throughput, surveys) drive disagreement.
States limitations or uncertainty of the evidence (sample size, short duration, rapid tool change, vendor funding).

objections.text: Many favourable results come from vendor-affiliated or vendor-funded studies.
Results from small or synthetic tasks do not generalise to large real-world codebases.
Self-reported speedups are unreliable; developers can feel faster while being measurably slower.
Findings about older tools/models may not apply to current ones because capability changes quickly.
Speed gains may be offset by downstream costs in review, defects, or maintenance.
